tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1: Build the ball-passing network of the Huskies season. Each player is a node, each pass a directed link. Identify network patterns at dyadic (pair), triadic (triple) and formation (position-block) levels, other structural indicators, across multiple spatial scales (micro pairwise to macro all-players) and time scales (minute-to-minute inside a match, whole match, whole season). Scope: 38 matches, 10,377 Huskies passes, 30 Huskies players, coordinates on a [0,100] attacking-perspective field.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) a pass row in passingevents.csv is one completed pass; self-passes (147 rows where origin=destination) are artifacts and removed; (b) field coordinates are already attacking-team oriented and normalized to [0,100], so pass length in field units is comparable across matches; (c) 2H events are offset by a 3300 s (55 min) half boundary to build absolute match time (observed 2H EventTime spans 0 to ~3441 s, consistent with ~57.4 min of second-half play); (d) the goalkeeper is part of the passing network but his role is coordination, so his near-zero same-position passing share is expected, not a defect. Method: directed weighted adjacency aggregated over the season for the macro view; directed dyads with reciprocity (return ratio) for the micro view; 3-player sets classified as undirected triangles, mutual (all 6 directed edges) and cyclic (containing a directed cycle) triads; origin-destination position blocks (G/D/M/F) for the formation view. This is sound because the data is a complete event log (23,282 valid passes of 23,429 after removing 147 self-passes; no missing geometry in passingevents.csv), so network counts are observed, not estimated.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let A be the 30x30 directed pass-count matrix, A_ij = number of passes i->j over the season; season total sum(A) = 10,377. Macro indicators: out-degree d_out(i)=sum_j A_ij; density = |{(i,j): A_ij>0}|/(30*29). Micro dyads: for each directed dyad (i,j), n_ij = A_ij, return ratio r_ij = A_ji/A_ij. Triads: for each 3-set {a,b,c} in which the undirected support is a triangle, let E be the set of the 6 possible directed edges; count mutual triads (|E_observed|=6) and cyclic triads (E_observed contains a directed cycle). Formation blocks: block share s_PQ = passes with origin position P to destination position Q, divided by total. Time scales: per-match subnetworks; 10-minute bins t_10 = floor(AbsTime/600); half (1H/2H); early window [0,900 s) and late window [4500 s, 5580 s]. Parameter table (empirical inputs): early_window = first 15 min of match, interval [10,20] min, source: expert exchange 3 (team shape becomes readable once each side has had enough possession, typically by 10-15 min and firm by 15-20 min); late_window = final 15 min, interval [15,20] min, source: expert exchange 5 (breakdown from loss of compactness usually shows in the last 15-20 minutes). All other numbers below are computed from the task dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Macro: 30 players, 635 directed links, density 0.730 — a highly connected network in which 10,377 season passes pass through 635 different directed pairs. The network is hubbed: top out-degrees are M1 (1248 passes), M3 (887), F2 (854), D1 (849), D3 (722); mean out-degree over non-zero nodes 345.9. Micro dyads: mean return ratio 1.19 (dyads are reciprocal on average — passes flow back and forth, the micro signature of a connected unit); the strongest dyads reach 182, 168, 143, 120, 117 season passes; among dyads with >=10 passes the highest return ratios are ~2.2-3.0 (clear two-way partnerships). Triads: 1,542 undirected triangles among 4,060 possible 3-sets (38% triangle rate); 709 of them contain a directed cycle, i.e. at least 46% of triangles show rotational ball flow (a-cb-a style) rather than a pure hub-spoke. Formation (position-block shares of season passes): D->M 14.6%, D->D 14.0%, M->D 16.1%, M->M 12.3%, D->F 9.6%, M->F 8.2%, F->D 6.3%, F->M 6.7%, F->F 2.8% — a midfield-mediated, defense-to-midfield heavy structure; the goalkeeper's rows are tiny (G->D 2.5%, G->F 1.3%, G->G 0). Role specialization: median player sends only 32.4% of passes to the same position line, so cross-line passing dominates; most positional senders are defenders (D10 50.0%, D2 49.3%, D1 45.2%), least positional are G1 (0%) and F2 (10.1%). Time scale: the same structural core (M1/M3/F2 hubs, reciprocal dyads) persists match-to-match, which is what makes the per-match indicators of Subproblem 2 well defined. Limitations: dyad/triad counts are descriptive, not causally weighted by success; the 55-min half offset is an assumption (data gives EventTime per half without added stoppage alignment); coordinates are rounded (integers in much of the file), limiting precision of distance-based inference; opponent-team structure is out of scope here by design (Huskies-centric question).

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2: Identify performance indicators of successful teamwork beyond points/wins — diversity of play types, coordination, distribution of contributions, plus team-level processes (adaptability, tempo, flow) — and use them to build a model capturing structural, configurational and dynamical aspects of teamwork. Scope: per-match indicators for the 38 Huskies matches, combined into a teamwork index and related to outcomes, home/away, and opponent strength (including whether strategies are universally effective or opponent-dependent).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) short, stable passing distance is the observable proxy for the connected-unit state that marks successful teamwork (expert exchange 1); (b) a match's early shape (first 15 min) is a fair early read of its teamwork (exchange 3); (c) late-game loss of compactness is the dominant breakdown mode (exchange 5); (d) contributions distributed across the squad, not a few stars, characterize winning teams (exchange 4); (e) tempo is situational — winning sides keep the same short-passing base with patient circulation and fast bursts, so average tempo is a weak, secondary indicator (exchange 7); (f) connection, not the position template, carries the season-level performance signal (exchange 10). Method: compute per-match indicators from cleaned pass data; standardize each (z-score over the 38 matches); form the teamwork index T as the equal-weight mean of standardized compactness (inverted), pass-type diversity, balance and tempo, plus T_def which drops tempo. Relate indicators to points (0/1/3), goal difference, side and opponent season strength. Soundness: all indicators are defined on the same event log, so comparisons are internally consistent; z-scoring removes unit effects; equal weighting is a deliberate, documented choice (no parameter fitted to the outcome, which would overfit on 38 points).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per match m with pass set P_m: compactness C_m = median_{p in P_m} L(p), L(p) = Euclidean distance between pass origin and destination in field units; diversity D_m = -sum_k q_k ln q_k, q_k the fraction of pass type k (7 types); balance B_m = 1 - Gini(n_i), where n_i is the number of passes initiated by player i in the match, Gini = (2 sum_i i n_(i))/(n sum_i n_i) - (n+1)/n over descending-sorted n; tempo R_m = |P_m| / (duration in minutes); forward bias F_m = share of passes with positive x-progress; early/late window values from the 15-min windows (table: early_window = 15 min, interval [10,20] min, source: exchange 3; late_window = final 15 min, interval [15,20] min, source: exchange 5). Standardization z(x) = (x - mean_m x_m)/sd_m. Teamwork index T_m = (z(-C_m) + z(D_m) + z(B_m) + z(R_m))/4; configuration-dynamics variant T_def,m = (z(-C_m) + z(D_m) + z(B_m))/3. Outcome link: Pearson correlation of each indicator with points; group means by outcome; context splits (home/away, first/second 19-game half, strong/weak half of opponents ranked by season points).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Correlations with points (n=38): late-window pass length -0.391 (strongest single indicator — late compactness collapse is the signature of losing matches); teamwork index T +0.270; early pass rate +0.259; balance +0.242; early pass length +0.224; T_def +0.194; tempo +0.171; late pass rate -0.150; diversity -0.039. Group means: T for wins +0.220 vs losses -0.004; T_def wins +0.172 vs losses -0.029. Fatigue window by outcome (late minus early median pass length): losses +1.78 (team stretches), ties +0.99, wins -1.92 (team gets tighter late) — matching the observed breakdown mode: losing Huskies matches disintegrate into long, disconnected passing in the final quarter. Early-shape diagnostic: the first 15 minutes carry real information (early length +0.224, early rate +0.259 with points), consistent with the practical rule that a team's shape is readable by 15 min. Tempo character: winning matches 2.93 passes/min vs losing 2.72, with forward bias nearly identical (0.564 vs 0.574) — winning is not driven by uniformly faster or more forward passing, supporting the 'same base, situational bursts' view; diversity of pass types is essentially uncorrelated with outcome (-0.04), so variety is not what separates results; balance of contributions is the strongest structural component (+0.242), i.e. the squad-wide distribution of work, not star passes, tracks wins. Adaptability: T is reasonably stable across contexts (within-context standard deviation 0.24-0.44 across home/away and season halves), so the index measures team behavior rather than a particular context. Opponent dependence: T correlates +0.310 with opponent season points, and T is higher vs the stronger half of opponents (+0.161) than the weaker half (-0.179) — the team's connection rises when required; this is a strategy that adapts to the counter-strategy rather than one universally fixed level of play. Limitations and biases: 38 matches is a small sample, so correlations of ~0.25-0.4 are suggestive, not decisive, and the 4-point scale (0/1/3) is coarse; z-scoring across only 38 values makes T sensitive to a few extreme matches; pass type 'diversity' is defined over 7 subtypes, some rare (Smart pass 190 season passes), so its entropy is noisy; balance is computed over initiators only and ignores receiving/pressing work, which the event data cannot fully reconstruct; T_def vs T is a design choice, not a fitted model, and no calibration against a golden standard exists in the data.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3: Use the teamwork model to advise the coach on which structural strategies have been effective for the Huskies and what network analysis indicates they should change next season to improve success. Scope: evidence-based recommendations grounded in the Subproblem 1-2 results, framed as next-season structural changes.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the coach can influence (a) defensive line depth and compactness in danger moments, (b) the squad's late-match fitness and rotation, (c) the set of recurring two-way passing partnerships, and (d) the early-game starting shape; the data cannot price individual player quality, so recommendations target network structure, not personnel. Approach: take the indicators that separate outcomes (late compactness -0.391 with points, balance +0.242, early rate/shape +0.22-0.26) and the stable structural facts (hub midfield, reciprocal dyads, midfield-mediated blocks, high D->M and D->D safety base) and translate each into an action with a measurable next-season target. The first-response norm under trouble — tighten the defensive shape, simplify to safe short passing (expert exchange 9) — is used as the prioritization order of the recommendations.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Decision rule: rank candidate changes by (i) strength of the outcome association of the indicator they move, (ii) stability of the current structural base that must not be broken, (iii) order of defensive-first prioritization. Current-state benchmarks computed from the data (next-season targets are relative to these): season median pass length 21.1 field units (1 field unit = 1% of pitch length); D->M 14.6% and M->D 16.1% of all passes; mean dyad return ratio 1.19; 1,542 undirected triangles (38% of 3-sets); late-window median pass length in losses = early + 1.78 vs wins = early - 1.92; balance (1-Gini of initiator passes) correlation with points +0.242; T (win mean) +0.220 vs (loss mean) -0.004.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Effective strategies to keep: (1) the midfield hub — M1/M3/F2 initiate 47% of season passes and anchor the reciprocal dyads; protect this triangle of partnerships (top dyads: 182, 168, 143 season passes each way is not the case, but the strongest 5 dyads carry 182/168/143/120/117). (2) The defense-to-midfield relay (D->M 14.6%, M->D 16.1%) is the team's safety base and the correct first line of response in trouble matches; do not remove it for directness. (3) Reciprocal short passing (mean return ratio 1.19) — the micro signature of the connected unit; winning matches get even tighter late, so keep that habit. Changes to make: (1) Highest priority — late-match compactness. Losing matches show pass lengths growing by ~1.8 field units in the final 15 min (fatigue collapse of the lines); target: in next season's last-15-min windows, median pass length in losing-or-trailing contexts should shrink, not grow (aim for the -1.9 pattern of wins), via fitness/rotation timing set at the 70-75 min mark (the window where breakdown usually starts) and a standing instruction to drop and compress when trailing. (2) Contribution balance. Balance of initiator passes tracks wins (+0.242); the current top 6 initiators produce ~56% of season passes while the bottom initiators contribute 65-137; target: raise the 25th percentile of per-match initiator counts, i.e. rotate secondary midfielders into the hub cycles so the Gini of initiator passes falls by a visible margin over the season. (3) Early-game shape. First-15-min pass rate and length are the best early predictors (+0.259/+0.224) yet early length in losses (19.9) is shorter than in wins (21.5) while rate is lower — losses start passive, not merely stretched; target: a fixed early-game possession trigger (e.g. early pass rate >= the season median of the win subset) as a self-check at the 15-min point, with the pre-agreed response being the safe short-pass circuit (the D->M->D base), consistent with the coach's usual first response to trouble. (4) Do not chase tempo or pass-type variety: tempo (+0.171) and diversity (-0.039) are the weakest levers, and winning matches already look like 'same base with faster bursts' rather than faster overall; next-season training tempo targets should keep the base short-pass tempo and add burst work. (5) Opponent-dependent play: T rises vs stronger opponents, so maintain the adaptive behavior; for weak opponents the T deficit (-0.179) suggests the team relaxes connection — keep the same connection standard (same early-shape check) regardless of opponent. Limitations: recommendations are correlational, from 38 matches, and assume the coach can measure the same indicators in-season; player-identity effects (who is fit, who is injured) are outside the data; the 70-75 min rotation timing is inferred from the 15-min late window and should be refined with minute-level next-season tracking.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4: Generalize the Huskies findings to team design in general: say something about how to design more effective teams, and identify what additional aspects of teamwork would need to be captured to build generalized models of team performance. Scope: cross-domain transfer of the network-and-dynamics findings, and a gap analysis for generalized team-performance modeling.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: treat the four validated findings — (a) connection (short stable inter-member distances / short reciprocal exchanges) is the season-level performance carrier, above the formal role template; (b) distributed contribution, not star concentration, tracks success; (c) the early window is diagnostic of the team's state; (d) failure is a collapse of compactness/coordination at the end or after sustained load — as structural claims about groups under sustained interaction, and map them to generic team processes. The mapping is qualitative by design: the soccer data validates the mechanics inside one controlled setting, and the generalization claims are the transferable ordering (connection > template; balance of contribution; early diagnostics; load-induced collapse), each tied back to a measured indicator so the generalization is anchored, not asserted.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Mapping (soccer indicator -> general team design principle): (1) compactness C (median exchange length, lower = tighter) -> maintain short, stable coupling distances between team members; design the team so every member has a near fallback (the 'always a nearby option' property), which in generic terms is: keep the effective communication/coordination cost per exchange below a team-specific baseline. (2) balance B = 1 - Gini(contributions) -> allocate workload so the Gini of contributions stays low; the squad, not a few stars, carries the load (credit concentrates in reporting, work distributes in performance — exchange 4). (3) reciprocity r_ij ~ 1.19 and cyclic triads (46% of triangles rotate) -> favor two-way exchanges and rotational subgroups over one-way hub-spoke chains, because reciprocal/cyclic structure is what lets the group re-route when a link fails. (4) early-window diagnostics (10-20 min read) -> any team can be sampled early in a task cycle; set an early-state checkpoint and a pre-registered corrective action rather than waiting for end-state failure. (5) late-window collapse (losses: +1.78 lengthening; wins: -1.92 tightening) -> the binding constraint in sustained team work is maintenance of coordination under load; build load management (rotation, recovery, simplification under stress) into the design. (6) adaptability: T stable across contexts (std 0.24-0.44) and higher vs stronger opponents -> a well-connected team functions under changing conditions; template-only teams do not. Parameter table (only empirical inputs reused from exchanges): early diagnostic window [10,20] min (exchange 3); collapse window final [15,20] min (exchange 5); new-member integration horizon ~5-10 task cycles (exchange 8) — used as the timescale over which a re-designed team should be judged. All other figures are from the task dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Generalized design principles: (i) invest in the connections between members, not in the formal template — the template (formation) is a starting constraint; the passing relationships inside it are what convert it into results, and this held season-level in the data. (ii) Engineer for distributed contribution; a low Gini of workload is a design target and a monitorable KPI. (iii) Instrument early checkpoints: the first ~15-20% of a task cycle reveals the team's coupling state, and the corrective should be pre-agreed (defensive teams: compress and simplify). (iv) Plan for the end of the task, not just the start: performance collapse is a load/coordination failure, so sustained teams need rotation and recovery engineered in, and 'tightening under pressure' (as the winning Huskies matches do) is the target behavior. (v) Keep the base process stable and add situational bursts; do not confuse variety or average speed with quality. Aspects that would need to be captured for truly generalized models: (a) the receiving/coverage side of interaction — soccer data only logs the ball carrier's pass, so defensive coverage, pressing, and non-carrying contributions (the invisible work that makes stars possible) are unobserved; generalized models need both directions of every interaction. (b) Emotional/motivational state and trust dynamics, which drive whether connections form and survive; (c) leadership and communication structure (here only proxied by the goalkeeper's coordination role and hub out-degree), including who sets tempo and how instructions propagate; (d) individual skill heterogeneity and how it is absorbed by the network (a star can win a single match against good organization — exchange 6 — so models must separate the distribution of ability from the distribution of work); (e) opponent/counter-strategy co-dynamics at the season level (only partially observed here via opponent strength); (f) the time course of learning and integration (new members need ~5-10 cycles, new tactics 4-8, a major change a full preparation block — exchange 8), which any generalized model must treat as a state variable; (g) multi-task and cross-context transfer, since adaptability was only tested within one sport and one season. Limitations of the generalization itself: single team, single season, single sport, 38 matches, ball-carrier-only observation; the transfer is a structurally-anchored hypothesis for further testing, not a validated cross-domain law; and the indicators are defined in the soccer domain, so each would need a domain-specific operationalization before use elsewhere.
